items.readable_text:
Content:
A circle is inscribed in an equilateral triangle if the circle touches all three sides of the triangle, as shown in the diagram below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/8a6a53b40f8ec8edcb8bcb784bf32a80]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll learn how to solve problems involving circles inscribed in equilateral triangles. Solving these kinds of problems often involves deducing key information from this diagram using our knowledge of angle bisectors and 30-60-90 triangles.

Content:
Let's see how we can create a 30-60-90 triangle from this setup.

Content:
First, suppose we draw the segments [MATH: \overline{OA},] [MATH: \overline{OB},] and [MATH: \overline{OC}] from the circle's center to each of the triangle’s vertices. By the SSS criterion, we get three congruent isosceles triangles, [MATH: \triangle{AOB},] [MATH: \triangle{BOC},] and [MATH: \triangle{AOC},] each with a central angle of [MATH: 120^\circ,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/1639ad87eabf6ae897aae0babb8e7738]

Content:
Now, suppose we draw the altitude [MATH: \overline{OM}] in [MATH: \triangle{AOC}] from the center of the circle to the point where the circle touches the opposite side. This divides the triangle into two right triangles, [MATH: \triangle{AOM}] and [MATH: \triangle{COM},] with angles [MATH: 30^\circ,] [MATH: 60^\circ,] and [MATH: 90^\circ.] The triangle [MATH: \triangle AOM] is shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/500ec5ae9dde5633a4deae2fdb95559a]

Content:
To successfully solve problems involving circles inscribed in equilateral triangles, it's essential to understand how to construct these 30-60-90 triangles effortlessly. So, let's get some more practice at this in a similar situation.

Therefore, all the statements are true.

Content:
Now, suppose that a circle of radius [MATH: 8 \: \text{mm}] is inscribed into an equilateral triangle, as shown below. How can we use this information to determine the triangle's side length?

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/b6c08bd5a9f3827f5668aad154db2284]

Content:
To find the side length of the triangle, we draw line segments from the center to each of the triangle’s vertices. This forms three identical isosceles triangles, each with a central angle of [MATH: 120^\circ,] as shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/294ded5d8984ff3c49c02d05834d60d8]

Content:
Now, we take one of these isosceles triangles and draw an altitude from the center to the opposite side. This divides the triangle into two right triangles with angles [MATH: 30^\circ], [MATH: 60^\circ], and [MATH: 90^\circ.]

Content:
In each [MATH: 30]-[MATH: 60]-[MATH: 90] triangle:

Content:
- Let the longer leg, which is opposite the [MATH: 60^\circ] angle, be [MATH: x.] Notice that it is half of our equilateral triangle's side length.
- The shorter leg is a radius of the circle with length [MATH: r = 8 \: \text{mm}.]

Content:
Recall that, in any [MATH: 30]-[MATH: 60]-[MATH: 90] triangle, the longer leg is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times the shorter leg:

Content:
[MATH: x|= r ⋅ sqrt(3); = 8 ⋅ sqrt(3); = 8sqrt(3)]

Content:
Therefore, our equilateral triangle's side length is
[MATH: 2x = 2 \cdot 8 \sqrt{3} = 16 \sqrt{3} \: \text{mm}.]

Content:
Let's now consider an example where we need to calculate the area of the equilateral triangle.

sections.normalized_html: A circle of radius [MATH: 7 \: \text{cm}] is inscribed into an equilateral triangle, as shown above. What is the area of the triangle?
sections.readable_text:
A circle of radius [MATH: 7 \: \text{cm}] is inscribed into an equilateral triangle, as shown above. What is the area of the triangle?

[IMG: /graphics/f9b826d3cb6a0bc6f73bcada108a2e55]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To find the side length of the triangle, we draw line segments from the center to each of the triangle’s vertices. This forms three identical isosceles triangles, each with a central angle of [MATH: 120^\circ,] as shown below.

Now, we take one of these isosceles triangles and draw an altitude from the center to the opposite side. This divides the triangle into two right triangles with angles [MATH: 30^\circ], [MATH: 60^\circ], and [MATH: 90^\circ.]

In each [MATH: 30]-[MATH: 60]-[MATH: 90] triangle:

  • Let the longer leg, which is opposite the [MATH: 60^\circ] angle, be [MATH: x.] Notice that it is half of our equilateral triangle's side length.

  • The shorter leg is the radius [MATH: r = 7 \: \text{cm}] of the circle.

Next, in the [MATH: 30]-[MATH: 60]-[MATH: 90] triangle, the longer leg is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times the shorter leg:

[MATH: x|= r ⋅ sqrt(3); = 7 ⋅ sqrt(3); = 7sqrt(3)cm]

Therefore, our equilateral triangle's side length is [MATH: s = 2 \cdot 7 \sqrt{3} = 14 \sqrt{3} \: \text{cm},] and the corresponding area of the triangle is [MATH: A|= (sqrt(3))/(4)s^{2}; = (sqrt(3))/(4)(14sqrt(3))^{2}; = (sqrt(3))/(4) ⋅ 588; = 147sqrt(3)cm^{2}.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

By the SSS criterion, we get three congruent isosceles triangles, [MATH: \triangle{AOB},] [MATH: \triangle{BOC},] and [MATH: \triangle{AOC},] each with a central angle of [MATH: 120^\circ,] as shown below.

This divides the triangle into two right triangles, [MATH: \triangle{AOM}] and [MATH: \triangle{COM},] with angles [MATH: 30^\circ,] [MATH: 60^\circ,] and [MATH: 90^\circ.] The triangle [MATH: \triangle AOM] is shown below.
